Because it treats the evidence regarding overall life expectancy as insufficient and mixed, the stance is hedged.

# Vegetarian Diets and Life Expectancy: What the Evidence Shows

**The claim is partially supported but overstated.** The evidence suggests vegetarian diets are associated with *some* mortality benefits, but the effect on overall life expectancy is more modest and disease-specific than a blanket "vegetarians live longer" claim implies.

**Key findings:**

A 2021 meta-analysis found vegetarian diets were associated with reduced risk of *ischemic heart disease mortality specifically*, but had **no significant effect on all-cause mortality** or cerebrovascular mortality — and the authors noted the certainty of evidence was low ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666667721000374)).

A comprehensive review of long-term vegetarian cohort studies similarly concluded that "overall mortality is similar for vegetarians and comparable non-vegetarians," though vegetarian groups do fare better than the general population, likely due to other healthy behaviors common among vegetarians (less smoking, more exercise) ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/proceedings-of-the-nutrition-society/article/longterm-health-of-vegetarians-and-vegans/263822873377096A7BAC4F887D42A4CA)).

However, the Adventist Health Study-2 — one of the largest and most rigorous cohorts, studying Seventh-day Adventists — did find vegetarian diets associated with **lower all-cause mortality**, with effects more pronounced in men ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23836264](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23836264/)).

**Interpretation:** Results are inconsistent across studies. This likely reflects the "healthy user bias" common in nutrition research — vegetarians often differ from meat-eaters in smoking, alcohol use, exercise, and socioeconomic status, making it hard to isolate diet as the causal factor. The strongest, most consistent finding is a reduced risk of cardiovascular/ischemic heart disease mortality, not necessarily overall life expectancy.

**Conclusion:** The claim is *directionally plausible* but not firmly established for all-cause mortality/life expectancy. Evidence is stronger for specific disease outcomes (heart disease) than for overall longevity, and study quality is generally rated low-to-moderate certainty.
